definition: The sky and the highest god in Turkic and Mongol traditions, often called the eternal blue sky. The Orkhon inscriptions and the Secret History invoke Tengri as the source of life and royal authority, though ideas about him vary widely.

A Turkic and Mongol goddess of fertility, childbirth and the hearth, protector of children and the womb. She appears in the eighth-century Orkhon inscriptions and is still invoked in Central Asian and Siberian traditions.

A heavenly hero of the Mongol, Buryat and Tibetan epic traditions, sent to defeat demons and restore order. Versions differ by language and religion, and the first printed text was a Mongolian woodblock of 1716.
The Kyrgyz heroic epic, performed by manaschi, telling of Manas, his companions and his descendants. It survives in many oral and written versions and is among the longest epic poems in the world.

The ruler of the underworld in Turkic and Mongol traditions, called Erleg in Mongolian. He is a cosmic power who receives the dead, sends sickness and can be approached with sacrifice, not simply a devil.

A ritual specialist in Mongol, Buryat and other Siberian traditions who enters altered states to heal, divine and journey between worlds. Practice varies widely, and Mongolian has separate words for male and female shamans.
The grassland belt of Eurasia, from the Hungarian plain to Manchuria, where pastoral nomads moved with their herds. It is a place and a cultural zone, not a single religion or people.
A long narrative poem or prose performance about heroes, often sung from memory. Steppe epics such as Geser and Manas are oral, formulaic and change with each performer.
A cairn of stones and offerings at a mountain pass, spring or sacred place in Mongolia and Buryatia. Travellers circle it, add stones and leave offerings to honour the local spirits.
A performer of the Kyrgyz epic Manas, who recites it from memory in a rhythmic chant. Great manaschi know the whole trilogy, and each shapes a version of the epic.
